questions.stem_html:
A 28-year-old laboratory technician reports progressive fatigue, recurrent mouth ulcers, and easy bruising. CBC shows pancytopenia with a very low reticulocyte count. There is no lymphadenopathy or splenomegaly. Bone-marrow biopsy is markedly hypocellular and largely replaced by fat; no malignant infiltrate or fibrosis is seen.

Which mechanism most commonly underlies acquired idiopathic disease of this type?

options.text_html: Sequestration and accelerated destruction of mature blood cells in an enlarged spleen
Cytotoxic T-cell-mediated suppression and destruction of multipotent hematopoietic stem cells
Monoclonal expansion of a myeloid precursor carrying BCR-ABL1
Autoantibody-mediated destruction restricted to circulating platelets
Defective DNA mismatch repair in mature erythrocytes

questions.explanation_html: Activated T cells release inhibitory cytokines and trigger apoptosis of hematopoietic stem and progenitor cells. Loss of all marrow lineages produces pancytopenia and low reticulocytes. The absence of organomegaly and the hypocellular fatty marrow localize the defect to stem-cell production rather than peripheral sequestration or lineage-specific destruction.

wrong_choice_explanations.1: Hypersplenism produces splenomegaly and does not cause a profoundly hypocellular fatty marrow.
wrong_choice_explanations.3: A clonal leukemia generally produces hypercellular or infiltrated marrow rather than empty fatty marrow.
wrong_choice_explanations.4: Immune thrombocytopenia causes isolated thrombocytopenia with preserved other lineages.
wrong_choice_explanations.5: Mature erythrocytes lack nuclei, and mismatch-repair defects do not produce global marrow aplasia.

questions.educational_objective: Identify aplastic anemia as a production failure caused commonly by immune attack on hematopoietic stem cells, producing pancytopenia, low reticulocytes, and a hypocellular fatty marrow.
